My objective in pursuing a PhD in Sustainable Development is to advance interdisciplinary research on digital finance to improve food security, incomes and climate-resilience among smallholder farmers in the global south. As a Foreign Service Officer with USAID, I witnessed firsthand the challenges in expanding opportunities for low-income farmers, as well as the resulting mass displacement due to worsening climate-related disasters. With the support of Columbia’s diverse experts, I hope to leverage novel methods combining remote sensing, agricultural economics, and AI-assisted surveys to help policymakers and social enterprises overcome barriers in financial access for remote agricultural communities. 

My diverse academic background and career have prepared me to develop novel applied research. As an undergraduate studying finance and economics, my research focused on a microfinance nonprofit in South Africa, analyzing how to leverage national empowerment policies to expand their lending portfolio among smallholder farmers. As a Fulbright Scholar in Germany, I was a visiting fellow at the Centre for European Economic Research, where I co-authored a working paper in German analyzing the integration progress of asylum seekers and presented the findings to the regional government. While studying for a Master’s in Development Practice at UC Berkeley, my research centered on applications of big data for climate-resilient agriculture. I developed a geospatial model for the Berkeley Food Institute using satellite-based evapotranspiration to analyze water scarcity risk for farmers in the Central Valley, while my advanced coursework included research projects on mapping multidimensional vulnerability through principal component analysis and predicting vegetation trends using harmonic forecasting of satellite imagery. My degree culminated with a thesis supervised by agricultural economists David Zilberman and Alain De Janvry, in which I applied a genotype-environment interaction framework to compare the accuracy of improved wheat yield predictions from a standard Bayesian generalized linear regression model with various machine learning approaches incorporating remote sensing data.

As a Foreign Service Officer with USAID, I applied my skills to directly improve the effectiveness of development programs in complex environments. As a visiting fellow in South Africa, I helped author USAID’s regional gender analysis report, identifying ways to better empower women and vulnerable groups, particularly in our agricultural, environmental, and health interventions. In Colombia, I created a model for processing high-resolution drone imagery that helped secure land titles for smallholder farmers. I also designed USAID’s first multi-program evaluation, demonstrating the benefits of layering land titling, microfinance, and crop insurance programs through an environmental vulnerability targeting approach. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, I volunteered to lead a six-person team of monitoring and evaluation specialists in Kyiv, where I managed dozens of complex assessments, including designing and securing funding for a randomized impact evaluation of a $450 million agribusiness financing project. With the dissolution of USAID, my goal in pursuing a PhD is to leverage my experience to help make interdisciplinary development research more accessible and applicable for policymakers and practitioners in low-income countries.

My motivation for pursuing a PhD at Columbia is to gain more formal academic training at the intersection of development economics, international policy, and environmental science, so I will be able to publish innovative research on digital credit and insurance solutions for farmers at risk of climate-related displacement. I would like to investigate how to improve digital credit scoring models for smallholder farmers by leveraging high-resolution geospatial data from satellite imagery and mobile phone records. I am interested in supplementing this fused data with AI-powered mobile surveys that help tailor financial solutions to the circumstances of individual households. Daniel Björkegren’s pioneering research with the AI and Development initiative matches many of my interests, particularly his work on manipulation-robust prediction and causal inference using hypothetical evaluations, which I hope to combine with chatbot-enabled surveys that elucidate more detailed qualitative responses on farmers’ choices that can be used to simulate counterfactuals in estimating their investment decisions. I would like to investigate the use of novel methodologies in LLM-based data processing and double-machine learning to combine the textual information from farmers’ responses to chatbot surveys with remotely measured environmental covariates to better target credit offerings. I hope to use this rich dataset to align digital finance with farm-specific input needs and repayment windows, as well as tailor climate-adaptation suggestions to reduce the likelihood of crop failure and displacement due to heat and water stress. Pairing the resulting model with insurance offerings based on the reduced risk of crop failure could help lower premiums and increase adoption among farmers, further improving their resilience to climate-based displacement by ensuring cash transfers are disbursed accurately and quickly. In addition to Professor Björkegren, my interest in digital technology and agriculture aligns with the recent work of Jeffrey Sachs and Nirupam Bajpai in e-agriculture programs and policy incentives for ICT solutions for development. The program’s emphasis on cross-department collaboration would also support my research portfolio, particularly through work with economists such as Jack Willis, with his focus on crop insurance and value chain microfinance, and scientists such as Alexander de Sherbinin who focus on climate-forced displacement.

Having worked directly in implementing complex global development programs, I believe deeply in the interrelations of social, economic, and environmental systems, and know that the Sustainable Development program would allow me the academic freedom to work across these disciplines that a pure economics degree would not. The cross-sectoral approach of SIPA and opportunity to collaborate with faculty from multiple departments would allow me to explore novel solutions in digital finance to advance the climate-resilience and prosperity of the world’s most vulnerable farming communities. After my doctoral studies, I plan to expand my academic research through a professorship, while supporting direct implementation by collaborating with development organizations like the World Bank, research collectives like CEGA, and policymakers in low-income countries. I would also pursue temporary appointments in future government or multilateral institutions, especially if a future administration re-engages meaningfully with foreign assistance. Columbia’s unique academic community is the ideal environment for me to return to applied research, so that I can help advance programs that advance a more sustainable, food-secure future.

Faculty 1 - [David Lobell](https://eiper.stanford.edu/people/david-lobell)

Reason:

My proposed research portfolio aligns almost perfectly with David Lobell’s pioneering work using satellite imagery and causal machine learning to study climate adaptations for agriculture. The principal research questions of the Lobell Lab comparing the effect on intensive crop yields of different investments are at the heart of my own interest in expanding the out-of-sample validity of experimental interventions in climate-smart agriculture. I believe his sectoral experience in climate and agriculture as well as his methodological focus on high-dimensional spatiotemporal datasets for causal inference and proxy estimation would be invaluable in informing my future research, as evidenced by his recent papers on evaluating crop rotations and high-resolution poverty measurement using satellite data and machine learning. His positions spanning key centers within the Stanford community would also help me collaborate with faculty from other disciplines, such as the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies and the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy and Research (SIEPR). Dr. Lobell’s direct experience working with the IPCC and his own public benefit corporation, AtlasAI, also mirrors the kind of direct application I would like to pursue through my work, not only publishing for an academic audience but also developing useful, accessible tools for policymakers and practitioners.

Faculty 2 - [Marshall Burke](https://eiper.stanford.edu/people/marshall-burke)

Reason:

Marshall Burke’s innovative work on the Environmental Hazard Adaptation Atlas inspired much of my own research interests in hierarchical meta-analysis for comparing climate-adaptive agricultural interventions. The contextual data and methodological approach of the Atlas is similar to my own proposal for comparing agricultural innovations, which would differ mostly by focusing on experimental panel data from prior impact evaluations in agriculture, rather than wildfires and extreme heat and cold. Collaborating with the ECHO Lab on the Atlas would be an invaluable first step in developing my own research approach to apply similar methods to a complementary set of interventions, which could in turn become part of the already well-developed Atlas interface. While his direct research focuses more on environmental factors such as extreme temperatures and air pollution, his methodological approach is quite similar to my proposal, particularly in the consideration of complex interconnected factors such as climate change, conflict, and economic shocks as well as the application of remote sensing in data-scarce environments. Dr. Burke’s focus on policy-relevant and directly applicable research also aligns well with my interest in extending my results to practitioners, especially his engagement with developing an accessible framework for geospatial intelligence through AtlasAI.

Faculty 3 - [Solomon Hsiang](https://eiper.stanford.edu/people/solomon-hsiang)

Reason:

Dr. Hsiang’s unique focus on cutting-edge methodological research and applied policy work aligns directly with my research interests in applying satellite imagery with machine learning to pressing questions of climate adaptation in agriculture in developing country contexts. His recent publications on the impact of climate change on global agriculture under different adaptation scenarios are thematically similar to my own focus on improving uptake of locally efficient agricultural technology, while his methodological contributions in accounting for unobservable heterogeneity using spatial first differences approaches the same problem I seek to overcome in context-specific heterogeneity biasing meta-analyses. We also share a passion for increasing the accessibility of machine learning in satellite imagery, as indicated by his recent publications and extensive work with [mosaiks.org](http://mosaiks.org); I would hope to both use the mosaiks API for my own research and publish open-source codebases leveraging it to create an accessible framework for other impact evaluations. Finally, his direct connection to implementation via the Global Policy Laboratory and Climate Impact Lab would provide both invaluable opportunities for collaboration and potentially a platform for sharing my research directly with policymakers and practitioners.

Faculty 4 - Jennifer (Jen) Burney

Reason:

Dr. Burney’s focus on designing and evaluating adaptation technologies for farmers aligns well with my own thematic research interest in extending locally specific climate-adaptive agricultural interventions. Her research group’s strengths in earth systems science, statistics, remote sensing, economics, and food security would be extremely informative for my own cross-disciplinary research, helping me to bridge sectoral silos while maintaining scientific rigor. She also considers the impacts of food production and consumption on mitigating climate change, a direction I have not yet considered, but would be an important additional lens to any recommendations of adaptation interventions in climate-smart agriculture. I am particularly interested in her recent proposals for “safety valve” institutions to coordinate between food production and climate mitigation, which would be directly relevant to the sort of multilateral institutions I hope to work with, such as the FAO. Her direct focus on eliminating hunger, rather than just boosting yields, also aligns well with my own interest in direct applicability of my research for the most vulnerable populations.

Statement of Purpose

My objective is to improve the targeting of climate-adaptive agriculture policies in the global south. As a Foreign Service Officer with USAID, I led the design and evaluation of dozens of bilateral development programs in South Africa, Colombia, and Ukraine, but with the worsening climate crisis threatening global food security and reduction in foreign aid budgets disrupting agricultural support worldwide, there is a pressing need for more efficient and impactful programs that can be implemented directly by national governments. I hope to pursue a PhD in Berkeley's Agricultural and Resource Economics program to drive innovations in empirical research on scaling up successful experiments and pilot programs of improved seed varieties that can be readily adopted by practitioners.

As an undergraduate studying finance and economics, my research focused on affordable housing and agricultural microfinance. Working with a neighborhood advocacy group in Macon, Georgia, I combined community surveys with statistical analysis of municipal property records to estimate the spillover effects of vacant properties and public housing investments. Presenting my findings to the city council, I successfully advocated for an expansion of affordable housing developments. Motivated by my experience using data to drive policy change, I volunteered with a microfinance nonprofit in South Africa, analyzing their lending portfolio and national empowerment policies to help expand credit access and land titles for smallholder farmers. I presented results from both projects at several national conferences, receiving invaluable feedback and confirming my passion for empirical research that benefits vulnerable communities. As a Fulbright Scholar in Germany, I was a graduate assistant at the Centre for European Economic Research, where I co-authored a working paper in German analyzing the results of two proprietary surveys on the integration progress of asylum seekers and presented the findings to the regional government. I also conducted independent research on national-level survey data using an instrumental variables approach to analyze the causal impact of education on refugee job placement, which I presented at the Fulbright Europe and Humanity in Action conferences.

After witnessing the destruction of the Paradise wildfire during the first semester at UC Berkeley, I shifted my research focus to quantitative methods for climate adaptation. My advanced coursework included research projects on mapping socioeconomic vulnerability using principal component analysis with Marta Gonzalez and predicting NDVI trends using harmonic forecasting of satellite imagery with Siamak Khorram. I taught several courses as a GSI, including a special research seminar on geospatial analysis in R for ESPM PhD candidates. With the Berkeley Food Institute, I developed a hydrological model using remote sensing data to analyze water scarcity risk for farmers in the Central Valley. My degree culminated with a thesis supervised by David Zilberman, Alain De Janvry, Siamak Khorram, and David Roland Holst, in which I replicated a genotype-environment interaction study by Jose Crossa and compared the accuracy of yield predictions from the original Bayesian generalized linear regression using manually collected environmental covariates with various machine learning approaches using remote sensing data.

As a Foreign Service Officer with USAID, I applied my skills to directly improve agricultural programs in complex environments. In Colombia, I led a land classification program using high-resolution drone imagery to help secure land titles for smallholder farmers in remote regions. After Russia’s full-scale invasion, I volunteered to lead a six-person team of monitoring and evaluation specialists in Ukraine and successfully championed a randomized impact evaluation for a $450 million agribusiness financing project in collaboration with CEGA. With the dissolution of USAID, I would like to return to applied research, to leverage my firsthand experience of development to improve policies and programs at a larger scale.

I am interested in research that improves the implementation of climate-adaptive agricultural technology at scale in low-income countries by using prior experimental pilots combined with high-resolution spatiotemporal data to predict target locations and varieties that provide the greatest yield improvements. Initial pilot studies for improved seeds that depend on average treatment effects can fail to account for heterogeneity as well as general equilibrium effects at scale. Deriving useful policy guidance from agricultural RCTs that can make a significant impact at the national level requires a different approach. I would like to examine how three promising methods can be combined: comparing panel results with environmental covariates and outcome proxies using high-dimensional spatiotemporal data and machine learning, synthesizing the results of multiple related trials through hierarchical meta-analysis, and randomized saturation designs to elicit general equilibrium effects.

Granular data from remote sensing, mobile phone records, and administrative datasets now allow for systematic analysis of contextual factors driving heterogeneity in treatment effects. Tamma Carleton’s work with unbiased parameter recovery from satellite imagery, Marco Gonzalez-Navarro’s use of deep learning on satellite imagery for land cultivation impacts, and Josh Blumenstock’s research combining novel data streams for algorithmic proxies and micro-estimates of poverty demonstrate this approach is feasible at scale. I am interested in combining these methods to develop an accessible framework to enrich panel data from individual seed trials with spatiotemporal covariates and proxy outcome measures. I hope to use the fused panel and spatiotemporal data to analyze heterogeneous treatment effects (HTEs) using causal machine learning methods, developing more granular subgroup analyses that can improve out-of-sample-area predictions when pilots are scaled up to different geographies. Vira Semenova’s econometric work on HTEs in high-dimensional panels and debiased machine learning would be essential for this line of work. 

I would also like to explore hierarchical meta-analyses of related interventions in improved seed varieties, using fused panel data to synthesize evidence from large bodies of research, like CEGA's IDEAL framework. This can help correct for publication and small-sample biases while also providing a greater variety of observations for predicting the impact of improved seeds in a new location. Randomized saturation designs employ a similar approach for a single experiment, by clustering the intensity of treatments by geographic sub-groups, to calculate the general equilibria consequences of a single intervention. I am interested in how the clustering approach of randomized saturations can be used to improve the general equilibrium estimation of HTEs across multiple trials using spatial meta-analysis, to simulate proxy saturation clusters and explore quasi-experimental equilibria.  These questions build on much of Edward Miguel’s research on meta-analyses, causal forests, and randomized saturation for scaling agricultural policy, as well as much of CEGA’s focus on extending RCT results beyond the geographic area of study.

I’m particularly interested in how the debiased predictions of heterogeneous treatment effects from the combined methods above can be used as informed priors for a Bayesian causal framework. Such a model could improve the simulated allocation of high-yielding varieties within a national-level program by estimating which seeds would produce the greatest gains where, allowing in-silico policy experiments that account not only for local effects but also provide more accurate inputs to a general equilibrium model that can account for factors in production, trade, and climate. By applying cost estimates for the seeds plus proxy estimates for yields, the model could even estimate cost-benefit ratios, enabling targeting prioritization and improving policy implementation. Such a Bayesian model could be updated as programs are expanded, enabling continuous impact evaluation and benchmarking, particularly when outcome proxies can be reliably measured through remote sensing.

To complement my research agenda, I would reinforce my coursework in agricultural and resource economics with additional studies in advanced remote sensing, machine learning, and genomic agriculture, collaborating with many of UC Berkeley’s world-leading scientific departments. I would be interested in working directly with the excellent labs and extension programs in ARE, particularly Ellen Bruno’s work on cooperative extension, to test the approach in practice over the course of my studies and throughout my subsequent career. After graduating from the ARE program, I would like to further my research with a post-doctoral position focused on the application of climate-adaptive seed varieties in developing countries, preferably collaborating with an implementing organization like the CGIAR consortium. I would then pursue a tenure-track position as an academic researcher, expanding my work on improving resilient agriculture adaptations by collaborating directly with organizations such as the World Bank and FAO, as well as research consortia like CEGA and J-PAL. From my prior experience as a graduate student at Berkeley, I know there is no better program than the Agriculture and Resource Economics Department to help apply cutting-edge economic research to issues of improving the targeted adoption of agricultural innovations for climate adaptation. With the help of Berkeley’s world-leading experts, I hope to synthesize promising avenues of remote sensing, econometrics, and agricultural extension into a portfolio that not only contributes to the field, but also directly supports policymakers and practitioners to advance a more sustainable, food-secure, and prosperous future.

Briefly tell us why you chose these faculty members and why you chose them in this rank order:

While my research interests align with many faculty in the department and across the university, Tamma Carleton’s direct focus using large geospatial data from remote sensing to study the relationship between climate change and economic development are most closely related to my interests. Her recent publication in Nature, “Impacts of climate change on global agriculture accounting for adaptation” captures the scope of the adaptation challenge for staple crops, while her methodological advances in satellite-based machine learning approaches would be invaluable for the spatiotemporal datasets I hope to leverage. Furthermore, her leadership in the Climate Impact Lab and CEGA would help facilitate invaluable opportunities for collaboration with other leading researchers.

Marco Gonzalez-Navarro would also be an ideal match for my research interests, given his focus on satellite imagery, agricultural interventions, and climate adaptation. His most recent paper, “Irrigation Infrastructure and Satellite-Measured Land Cultivation Impacts: Evidence from the Senegal River Valley” marks a major contribution in the exact sort of causal evaluation of climate-adaptive agriculture using large scale spatiotemporal data that I hope to focus on. His methodological fluency in deep learning as applied to satellite imagery for impact evaluation, particularly for the estimation of poverty proxies based on housing quality, would be invaluable for my own research agenda. 

Ellen Bruno’s focus on applied agricultural extension research and empirical modeling for policy decisions would also be highly relevant to my ultimate goal of influencing the implementation of climate-adaptive agricultural practices at scale. While her work focuses more on California and specifically on groundwater management, her approach to stakeholder engagement and interdisciplinary collaboration is a model I hope to emulate in my own applied research. Her support in grounding my research in a way directly applicable to extension services and policy implementation would be a useful foundation for my portfolio.

I ranked Tamma Carleton and Marco Gonzalez-Navarro as my top preferences given their close thematic and methodological linkages to my proposed research portfolio. It was difficult to determine which would be the most relevant, but I believe Professor Carleton’s direct focus on large-scale climate adaptive agriculture is more closely tied to my meta-analytic approach, while Professor Gonzalez-Navarro’s approach is better suited to impact evaluations for a specific intervention and geography. Professor Bruno’s work is less directly connected to my interests methodologically, but her approach to research aligns well with my focus on immediately applicable and engaged scholarship. It would be an honor to collaborate with any of the ARE faculty, however, and given the interdisciplinary nature of the program I know that I would be able to engage with many relevant faculty at Cal.

Research Notes

- Combination of heterodox economics with novel empirical methods, focused on real-time / big data, to get away from neoclassical “small world” models based on assumptions and methodological frameworks. 
	- Investigate “what the data is saying” to determine “what is going on here” and interpret that according to various economic rationales, presenting various options of interpretations, historical parallels, and policy recommendations based on related evidence
- Development economics without the patronizing approach to “developing” economies, with a focus on intra-national disparities, to improve equity and safeguards / programs for vulnerable / low-income / at-risk people
- Focus on applications in policy / programs / interventions, not just theories; contextually situated cases, not global assumptions
	- Focus on both domestic issues locally and in areas where I have cultural competency (South America, Eastern Europe)
- Culturally sensitive / non-imperialist economics that doesn’t assume Western enlightenment moral foundations for utilitarianism
	- Using local language, dissemination
- Focus on improving policies / programs / interventions for working class rather than “macroeconomic stability” for investors and capitalists
	- Investigating wage stagnation and oligopoly power in rich world
	- Impacts of AI and technology on work / labor / unemployment
- Methodological focus on diverse data analysis, beyond traditional econometrics and panel data; mixed methods using NLP / LLM to supplement quant / admin data
	- Away from “average” effects, national statistics, “optimizing” solutions
	- Towards particular targeting, distributional effects, impacts on vulnerable
	- Accountability to results / progress via rigorous MEL focus

Based on the research I have gathered, The New School has several active research centers and institutes that focus on international development, public policy, social welfare, and economics. These centers serve as hubs for interdisciplinary research and public debate.

Public Policy and Social Welfare

* The Center for New York City Affairs: This center is an applied policy research institute that drives innovation in social policy, with a focus on how public policy affects low-income communities.[1, 2] It produces in-depth, original studies on issues like chronic absenteeism in public schools and the rising number of children in homeless shelters.[1, 2] The center's work aims to illuminate injustices and propose workable solutions.[1]

 * The Institute on Race, Power and Political Economy: Founded in 2021, this institute is a cross-disciplinary hub that advances research on structural inequalities and works to identify new ways to promote equity.[3, 4, 5] It draws on faculty from across the university to improve the understanding of stratification in areas such as education, employment, criminal justice, and housing.[4]

 * The Tishman Environment and Design Center: While its primary focus is environmental issues, the center is a hub for environmental and climate justice research and practice, integrating design, policy, and social justice.[6, 7] It conducts data-driven research, for example, creating a database on policies to address the cumulative impacts of environmental stressors on environmental justice communities.[6]

 * The Urban Systems Lab (USL): This interdisciplinary lab focuses on improving life in cities by studying the interactions between social, ecological, and technical systems.[8] It aims to develop data-driven tools and transformative strategies to address social and environmental challenges that contribute to inequity and injustice in cities worldwide.[9]

Economics

 * The Schwartz Center for Economic Policy Analysis (SCEPA): This is an economic policy think tank within the Department of Economics that focuses on the government's role in raising living standards, creating economic security, and achieving full employment.[10] It conducts original, standards-based research on key policy issues to empower policymakers and drive positive change.[10]

 * The Heilbroner Center for Capitalism Studies: This center brings together faculty and students for interdisciplinary conversations on the study of capitalism in its various forms.[11] It aims to develop theoretical and analytical tools to envision and promote "different and better economies".[11, 12] The center's research includes the relationship between capitalism and democracy and how power relations influence economic outcomes.[12]

International Development

 * The Julien J. Studley Graduate Programs in International Affairs: This program is designed to cultivate "engaged, reflective global citizens" to help address pressing global challenges such as refugee crises and climate change.[13] The programs are described as "critical, engaged, and truly global," emphasizing a pluralistic approach to international issues.[13]

* The Observatory on Latin America (OLA): Housed within the Graduate Programs in International Affairs, OLA is a research and practice center that fosters public debate on social reform in the Western Hemisphere.[14, 15] Since 2006, it has become a platform for disseminating and discussing Latin American ideas and has hosted over 150 events.[14] The center's programs include "Latin America on the Move," "Design and Development," and a "Cuba Program".[14, 15, 16]

Personal Statement

	My objective has always been to alleviate poverty by strengthening development programs with rigorous, relevant evidence. As the climate crisis increasingly threatens global food security, I am driven to pursue a PhD in Economics and Public Policy at Tufts to advance applied research on foreign policy that supports climate-adaptive agriculture in low-income countries. The program’s joint focus on development, climate, and policy is perfectly suited for my research goals and my diverse background combining economics, data science, remote sensing, and global development.

__Previous Experiences Motivating Doctoral Studies__

In 2008, my parents both lost their jobs and our house was foreclosed on. I was just starting high school, but my family had to move from shelters to motels for months as my parents looked for work. With only high school educations themselves, living in rural Georgia, there were few stable opportunities in the midst of a recession. The whole time, they repeated how important it was that I go to college, so I wouldn’t face this sort of instability again. I threw myself into my studies and volunteered for every extracurricular I could to boost my chances for college admissions. When my parents told me I’d have to quit Boy Scouts because we couldn’t afford the dues, my Scoutmaster offered to cover them instead; when I struggled in classes, my teachers stayed after school to tutor me. The most important lesson I learned from this difficult time was not just the value of education, but also the centrality of selfless mentors and a supportive community.

Which is why, when I was not only admitted to my nearby university, but also offered a full-tuition scholarship, I knew I had to find a way to pay that kindness forward. I studied finance and economics, determined to learn what exactly a “real estate crash” was and how it had devastated my family, but my faculty were more interested in promoting free market capitalism and maximizing portfolio returns. Ideologically frustrated with my coursework, I began tutoring at a local high school, where I realized that the root of many students’ problems were housing and food insecurity. Macon, Georgia was still bitterly segregated, with dilapidated houses and under-resourced schools holding back large parts of the city. Looking for a way to drive more sustainable change, I started volunteering with local neighborhood associations advocating on these issues to the municipal government. Working together with local leaders, I surveyed community members at church breakfasts and school meetings to present a case for better public services and investments in affordable housing, but the results weren’t “rigorous” enough to move the city councilors. I walked down the hall to the property assessor’s office and asked for real estate data; they gave me a thumb-drive full of spreadsheets and shapefiles containing property values and real estate transactions. Returning to my university, I found a public health professor willing to show me the basics of QGIS and R; with her help, I developed an analysis of historical land values across the city, using a spatial linear model to predict the property tax benefits of renovating dilapidated houses and building new units. In hindsight, it wasn’t very econometrically valid, but it was enough to persuade the city council, who voted in favor of our proposal to renovate several blocks into affordable public housing.

The experience validated for me the power of empirical evidence to inform public policy--that even imperfect research could advance social justice and help families like mine. Eager to expand my horizons and help communities beyond Georgia, I spent two summers volunteering with a microfinance group in South Africa, conducting research on Black Economic Empowerment policies and analyzing local agribusiness financial statements to help them extend credit to smallholder farmers. I went on to present my work from Macon and South Africa at several national conferences, where I was both applauded for my community focus and excoriated for my lack of theoretical rigor. I realized that the limited resources of my small university weren’t sufficient for me to learn what I needed; I needed a graduate education to really make a difference with research. With the help of yet more supportive mentors in the German and International Affairs department, I applied to every graduate fellowship I could, and ended up earning three. My summer after graduating started in Amsterdam, where I joined an international cohort of activists as a Humanity in Action Fellow to debate case studies in social justice issues and volunteer with Amnesty International and the Anne Frank Foundation. I then spent three months in Washington as a Donald Payne Fellow, where I worked in the Democratic Caucus and office of Congressman Joe Crowley conducting policy research, to prepare for my future career with USAID.

Thanks to the Fulbright Scholarship, I spent the following year auditing advanced courses at the University of Heidelberg and working as a graduate assistant at the Centre of European Economic Research (ZEW), learning Stata and econometrics while collaborating with a team focused on policies to support the integration of asylum seekers. My role was initially limited to data processing and visualization, but as I learned more advanced methods I sought out additional data to complement our regional survey, eventually adding useful context information from a nationally representative sample to our work. It was enough to be listed as co-author for our working paper, which we then presented to several city and provincial councils, but I still felt like the research wasn’t sufficient. In collaboration with a local advocacy group, led by Syrian and Afghan refugees, I translated my findings into grant applications to expand their job placement support programs. I also pursued my own independent research, applying an instrumental variables approach to estimate the impact of education and language courses on employment among refugees nationally. While my approach was theoretically sound, the limited variation within questions on language capability and vocational training precluded the kind of significant results that would have yielded conclusive, publishable evidence.

After Fulbright, I began my Masters of Development Practice degree at UC Berkeley, where I explored both the interdisciplinary nature of sustainable development and more advanced quantitative methods. I taught myself Python and JavaScript in addition to my coursework and teaching responsibilities, seeking to apply more advanced machine learning methods. When the Paradise wildfires tore through northern California, I realized that the worsening climate crisis was going to be a driving factor in the conflict, forced migration, and poverty that I hoped to address. Following another summer in South Africa working with USAID on climate-adaptive agriculture and environmental conservation, I dedicated my research to studying water scarcity for farmers in California’s central valley, applying methods from remote sensing, hydrology, and land classification to develop an interactive dashboard for the Berkeley Food Institute. I extended this work through my thesis, in which I explored the applicability of remote sensing data and machine learning to supplement a genotype-environment interaction study on heat- and drought-resistant wheat varieties. My favorite experience at Berkeley, however, was leading a weekly seminar each semester for the Data Scholars, a cohort program for students underrepresented in STEM to conduct research. I was proud that I could help other first generation students gain the research skills to pursue their own further education, to develop a welcoming community for those who, like me, felt like they didn’t belong in academia.

I graduated from Berkeley in the middle of the COVID-19 pandemic, swearing into USAID as a diplomat via video call. My initial rotations were conducted virtually, but I still managed to contribute to important processes, leveraging my data science background to streamline budget management negotiations and develop a visualization dashboard that helped catch several million dollars in misallocated funding. Recognizing the value of further quantitative skills in international development, I also began studying online for two more graduate degrees simultaneously, in mathematics and computer science. These proved immediately useful in my first overseas assignment in Colombia, where I developed a computer vision model for land classification using high-resolution drone imagery that helped hundreds of smallholder farmers in remote locations receive land titles. I also served as the Gender and Inclusive Development lead, ensuring our entire portfolio integrated best practices in the inclusion of women, LGBTQI+, Afro-Colombian and indigenous populations. With Russia’s full-scale invasion the following year, I volunteered to a special assignment leading the Monitoring and Evaluation team in Ukraine, again leveraging my diverse skillset to advocate for more econometrically robust impact evaluations and develop a remote third-party monitoring system that combined satellite imagery, mobile surveys, and video calls to conduct mandatory oversight without risking staff on the frontlines. Combining this with the new inventory database system I developed with our partners, I was able to build a real-time analytics dashboard to track electrical grid repairs, a tool that was used in briefings to the Ukrainian government and the U.S. National Security Council.

__Objectives for Applying to Doctoral Studies__

With the dissolution of USAID and broader retrenchment of international development, I have had to reconsider my purpose. Reflecting on my original motivations, I’ve realized that my passion lies in higher education; both in conducting meaningful applied research and supporting an inclusive community for other students from underprivileged backgrounds. My experiences with USAID confirmed the importance of rigorous evidence for impactful programs, as well as the challenges that practitioners face in adapting often abstract academic research to their purpose. Supplemental 1: Research Question

My research seeks to answer a critical question for climate adaptation: how can we accurately predict which interventions will work best for smallholder farmers in dynamic, heterogeneous contexts? The effectiveness of adaptation strategies, from drought-resistant seeds to irrigation, varies dramatically by location, yet most impact evaluations rely on random assignment to estimate average effects, omitting many contextual variables that explain heterogeneity and enable subgroup analysis. By relying on naive comparability assumptions, predicted treatment effects in new locations are likely biased, particularly given the temporal dynamics of climate change.

Granular data from remote sensing and administrative datasets allow the systematic analysis of contextual factors driving heterogeneity, as demonstrated in much of David Lobell’s research leveraging large-scale satellite data to study climate-smart practices in agriculture and the Adaptation Atlas led by Marshall Burke in the ECHO Lab. I hope to build on these methods by extending an accessible model similar to Solomon Hsiang’s mosaiks framework into crop yield and income proxies, fusing them with panel data from previous experiments, and using causal machine learning to conduct improved subgroup analyses. By connecting previously disparate trials into a joint evidence framework using common geospatial covariates, the model would allow more robust hierarchical meta-analysis to help correct for publication and small-sample biases in climate-adaptive agricultural interventions. Using the resulting de-biased effects as conditional priors, I plan to construct a Bayesian causal framework that can make robust out-of-sample predictions for novel locations and dynamic climate forecasts.

Investigating these techniques requires a multidisciplinary approach given the combination of complex environmental datasets, agricultural extension policy, development economics, and advanced statistical methodologies involved. Rather than narrowly investigate a single adaptation solution, I would like to improve comparability between past experiments from different disciplines, to increase their applicability for decision-making by practitioners. The PhD in Environment and Resources through E-IPER, with its many faculty focused on applied open-source frameworks and large-scale climate and agriculture models, would best support my research by enabling me to explore the intersection of related disciplines while developing my core environmental research skills. The Stanford academic environment would be perfectly suited for my research interests, particularly the Center on Food Security and the Environment with its emphasis on data science and climate adaptation.

Beyond publishing my results in a series of papers, I plan to regularly update a reproducible codebase that other researchers and partner organizations can leverage to improve impact evaluations. Ultimately, I would like to develop an interactive tool similar to the Adaptation Atlas that local cooperatives and extension services could use to select appropriate interventions and continuously monitor their progress. The final product would also allow practitioners at organizations like FAO or the World Bank to conduct in-silico policy experiments—inputting a project location and timeline to predict different interventions' disaggregated impacts on yields and poverty. By enabling more precise, data-driven targeting of climate adaptation funds, this work can help ensure that limited resources are directed to the most appropriate interventions that will have the largest impact on food security and climate resilience.

My research interests center on two questions: how to better leverage prior experimental results to inform cash transfer program design in the face of heterogeneity, and how to improve outcome monitoring for programs in remote locations. Comparing ground-truth data from prior surveys with relevant covariates and income proxies from satellite imagery, weather models, and mobile phone records has been shown to generate more contextually and temporally granular measures of impact, while also providing more cost efficient methods of passive data collection for program monitoring. I am also interested in combining multiple trials at the household level through hierarchical meta-analyses to help overcome small-sample and publication biases for related interventions, while also introducing useful covariate heterogeneity. Novel methods for subgroup analysis, such as concave fusion penalization, would also be interesting to test across studies, to extend a synthetic control framework between subgroups which are too small in individual samples but become significant in pooled data. Isaiah Andrews pioneered such methods in metastudies for overcoming publication bias and evaluations of external validity, so I would be eager to collaborate with him in my research. I would also like to investigate how the resulting harmonized data could be analyzed using novel econometric methods such as generalized additive models, double-machine learning, and causal forests to estimate robust heterogeneous treatment effects and complex variable interactions. Victor Chernozhukov’s extensive research on high-dimensional data established many of these approaches, while Alberto Abadie’s research on causal inference in data-rich environments using latent factor models and local principal subspace approximations defined the theoretical framework for such computational approaches to nonlinear modeling.

My motivation for pursuing a PhD in Public Policy in the Economics track at the Kennedy School is to help prepare for the revitalization of American foreign assistance. I am interested in researching politically tractable solutions for interagency standards on designing, implementing, and measuring assistance programs based on their combined benefits to Americans and partner nations, so funding can be allocated to maximize impact according to national security priorities. Academic Statement of Purpose

I would like to pursue a PhD in Public Policy and Economics at Michigan so that I can contribute to applied research on city- and state-level immigration policies that improve economic mobility and housing security for low-income communities.

As an undergraduate studying finance and economics in Macon, Georgia, my research and advocacy focused on expanding investments in affordable housing and microenterprises. Working with a local neighborhood advocacy group, I combined community surveys with spatial analysis of property records to estimate return-on-investment in affordable housing for local tax revenues, leveraging my findings to persuade the city council to invest in low-income neighborhoods. Witnessing similar deprivation abroad, I volunteered for a microfinance nonprofit in South Africa, analyzing national policies and loan records to help expand credit access for small businesses. I presented findings from both projects at several national conferences and received multiple graduate fellowships to support my continued education and advocacy. Thanks to the Payne Fellowship, I interned in the House of Representatives, where I developed a quantitative model to assess a major pension reform bill and authored several position papers on international issues for the Democratic Caucus. As a Fulbright Scholar in Germany, I focused on job placement and language training for asylum seekers, working at the Centre for European Economic Research to co-author a working paper and present the findings to the regional government. I also conducted independent research using an instrumental variables approach to estimate the causal relationship between education on job placement among refugees, which I presented at the Fulbright Europe and Humanity in Action annual conferences. Seeking to make a more immediate impact, I also volunteered with a local nonprofit focused on vocational and language training for asylum seekers, translating my research findings into a series of grant applications to help them expand their programs. I continued my studies with a Master of Development Practice at UC Berkeley, where I focused on climate adaptation, data science, and teaching quantitative methods. Returning to South Africa for a summer practicum, I worked with USAID on programs to help manage regional migration, focusing on gender-based violence prevention and reducing transmission of HIV among migrant communities. There is no better program than the Joint PhD in Public Policy and Economics at Michigan to help me apply cutting-edge economic research to complex issues of economic mobility, housing affordability, and migration management. With the help of Michigan’s world-leading experts, I hope to develop novel research that not only contributes to the field, but also directly supports migrants and low-income communities.

My motivation for pursuing a PhD at Stanford is to combine my applied experience in international development with environmental research on climate-adaptive agriculture to improve extension of relevant innovations to vulnerable farmers. My research interests align perfectly with the work of scholars at the Center on Food Security and the Environment, particularly David Lobell’s work using large-scale satellite data to study climate-smart practices in agriculture, Solomon Hsiang’s research on unobservable heterogeneity in spatial models, and Brandon de la Cuesta’s Climate Impacts for Social Science Computing Platform.

heading_path: ML Global Approximations vs. Causal Interpretability in Dynamic Models
text: # ML Global Approximations vs. Causal Interpretability in Dynamic Models __The Core Problem: Dimensionality vs. Interpretability__ - __The Grid Trap:__ Traditional global solution methods (like splines) suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Attempting to solve a model with dozens of interacting variables (e.g., massive spatiotemporal climate and agricultural state spaces) creates an exponentially uncomputable hypercube. - __The ML Solution:__ Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) bypass this using __mesh-free__ approximation. By stochastically sampling the ergodic set (where the system actually spends its time) and using gradient descent to minimize equation errors, DNNs easily solve high-dimensional systems. - __The Black Box Trade-off:__ While DNNs provide unprecedented global accuracy, they destroy mechanistic interpretability. You lose the cleanly defined partial derivatives required to isolate marginal effects and defend specific causal policy interventions. __The Pitfalls of Uncertainty & Bias__ - __Epistemic Uncertainty:__ We can map a DNN's ignorance using Monte Carlo simulations (e.g., Monte Carlo Dropout) to find where prediction errors blow up—usually during rare, extreme shocks outside the ergodic set. This yields *reliability* (we know where the model is guessing) but still fails to recover causal mechanisms. - __Spectral Bias (The Danger Zone):__ Neural networks naturally prioritize learning smooth, generalized, low-frequency functions. In environmental and economic systems defined by sharp, highly non-linear thresholds (like sudden ecological collapses or critical agricultural tipping points), the DNN will likely "smooth over" the crisis, embedding a dangerous structural bias into its predictions. __Potential Research Question (The Frontier):__ How can we bridge the gap between computational power and structural econometrics? Specifically, can we design loss functions or hybrid architectures that force mesh-free ML algorithms to mathematically respect sharp, non-linear ecological tipping points while maintaining the rigorous causal inference needed to evaluate sustainable development interventions?

text: # Microeconomic Optimization Alternatives to Theoretical Analytic Approaches The tension between structural analytical modeling and non-parametric or data-driven optimization is a central methodological debate in modern econometrics and quantitative economics. Your assessment is correct: the traditional analytical Lagrangian paradigm requires the ex-ante specification of a functional form (e.g., Cobb-Douglas, CES, Translog), meaning the resulting optimization is conditional on those structural assumptions. When starting directly with observed data from an economy, bypassing rigid functional forms to avoid misspecification bias is a primary motivation for utilizing alternative mathematical toolkits. However, the solution is generally not to apply heuristic search algorithms like hill climbing to the raw data, but rather to use __shape-constrained non-parametric estimation__ or __algorithmic data-driven optimization__. The comparative benefits, mathematical trade-offs, and methodology of optimizing without preconditioning on an assumed functional form are structured as follows:

heading_path: Microeconomic Optimization Alternatives to Theoretical Analytic Approaches
__1. Non-Parametric Optimization: Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA)__
text: ## __1. Non-Parametric Optimization: Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA)__ If your objective is to evaluate profit maximization or cost minimization for a firm producing $n$ products using $m$ inputs without assuming a production function $f(x)$, the standard economic approach relies on __Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA)__ or __Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA)__. Instead of assuming a specific algebraic form, DEA uses linear programming to construct an empirical production possibility frontier directly from the observed input-output vectors of all firms in the data. - __The Mathematical Mechanism:__ Axiomatic properties derived from microeconomic theory—such as monotonicity (inputs are goods) and convexity of the technology set—are imposed as linear inequality constraints. The optimization problem for a specific firm's efficiency score $\theta^*$ is formulated as a linear program: - $$\begin{aligned} \text{maximize } & \theta \\ \text{subject to } & \sum_{j=1}^{J} \gamma_j y_{nj} \ge \theta y_{n0}, \quad \forall n=1, \dots, N \\ & \sum_{j=1}^{J} \gamma_j x_{mj} \le x_{m0}, \quad \forall m=1, \dots, M \\ & \gamma_j \ge 0 \end{aligned}$$ - where $y_{nj}$ and $x_{mj}$ are the observed outputs and inputs of firm $j$, and $\gamma_j$ represents the weights used to construct the virtual peer firm. - __The Benefit:__ This is a purely data-driven numerical optimization. It completely avoids functional misspecification bias while remaining entirely disciplined by economic theory (convexity and monotonicity). Because it maps to a linear program, it is solved exactly using the Simplex or Interior Point methods, bypassing the inefficiencies of heuristic search algorithms.

1. Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) in Python
text: ### 1. Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) in Python To execute non-parametric optimization directly on observed economic inputs and outputs (bypassing functional forms like Cobb-Douglas), researchers use specialized solvers that wrap linear programming APIs. A prominent library for this is __Pyfrontier__ (or alternatively pyDEA), which handles the optimization loop over individual Decision Making Units (DMUs) using PuLP or SciPy backends.

__2. Shape-Constrained Non-Parametric Econometrics__
text: ## __2. Shape-Constrained Non-Parametric Econometrics__ A closely related alternative is to estimate the unknown utility or production function non-parametrically using the observed data, while explicitly constraining the estimator to satisfy structural economic axioms. - __Methodology:__ Rather than estimating a standard unconstrained polynomial or kernel regression—which can yield non-monotonic or non-concave functions due to finite-sample noise—you solve a __Shape-Constrained Kernel Estimation (SCKE)__ or __Sieve Estimator__ problem. - __The Optimization Problem:__ The estimator minimizes the sum of squared residuals subject to the mathematical requirements that the first derivative is non-negative and the second derivative matrix (Hessian) is negative semi-definite at all data points: - $$\begin{aligned} \text{minimize } & \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( y_i - \hat{f}(x_i) \right)^2 \\ \text{subject to } & \nabla \hat{f}(x_i) \ge \mathbf{0}, \quad \nabla^2 \hat{f}(x_i) \preceq \mathbf{0} \quad \forall i \end{aligned}$$ - __The Numerical Framework:__ This optimization cannot be solved analytically via standard Lagrangians because $\hat{f}$ lives in an infinite-dimensional function space. Instead, it is projected onto a finite-dimensional basis (sieves) and solved numerically using __Semi-Definite Programming (SDP)__ or __Constrained Spline Optimization__.

text: ### 2. Shape-Constrained Optimization (Imposing Curvature Constraints) If you choose to use data-driven methods but need to ensure the estimated function complies with microeconomic axioms (such as marginal utility diminishing with consumption, meaning a strictly concave function where $\nabla^2 f \preceq 0$), simple unconstrained regressions fall short. The library __gamfit__ (or shape-constrained additive models in packages like scikit-shapes or R's scam) solves this by binding the regression coefficients via inequality constraints during optimization.

The Optimization Loop Mechanics
text: #### The Optimization Loop Mechanics If you look into the core source code of shape-constrained optimization engines (often written in optimized backends like C++ or Rust to speed up loop execution), the library sets up a penalised spline objective. To enforce shape=concave, the package sets up a system of second-difference matrix inequalities on the spline coefficients vector $\beta$: $$\mathbf{D}_2 \beta \le \mathbf{0}$$ It then passes this system to a __Quadratic Programming (QP)__ solver using active-set or interior-point methods. The solver steps through iterations until it minimizes the squared errors while strictly keeping the KKT stationarity conditions within the feasible, concave boundaries.

__3. Structural vs. Non-Parametric: The Methodological Trade-offs__
text: ## __3. Structural vs. Non-Parametric: The Methodological Trade-offs__ If non-parametric numerical methods allow you to optimize without assuming a functional form, why do structural analytical models persist? The choice depends on the trade-off between __internal validity (robustness to misspecification)__ and __counterfactual policy invariance__. __Dimension__ __Structural Analytical Approach (Assumed Functional Form)__ __Data-Driven / Non-Parametric Numerical Approach__ __Misspecification Bias__ __High risk.__ If the true technology is translog but you assume Cobb-Douglas, your optimization results and elasticity estimates will be fundamentally biased. __Minimal risk.__ The data dictates the shape of the frontier or function; the model adapts to arbitrary curvatures. __Data Requirements__ __Low.__ Can calibrate parameters (e.g., share parameters $\alpha$) using a small number of empirical moments or baseline data points. __High.__ Non-parametric convergence rates suffer from the "curse of dimensionality" as the number of inputs $m$ and outputs $n$ increases. __Counterfactual Analysis__ __High capacity.__ Because the parameters capture invariant deep structural primitives (e.g., risk aversion, technological substitution elasticity), you can simulate behavior under entirely new economic regimes or out-of-sample price shocks (__Lucas Critique__ compliance). __Limited capacity.__ Non-parametric frontiers are only valid within the support of the observed data. They cannot reliably predict optimization behavior under an unprecedented policy shock or price regime. __Economic Interpretability__ __Direct.__ Multipliers map explicitly to shadow prices; parameters map to marginal rates of substitution. __Indirect.__ Results are often represented as empirical efficiency distributions or localized numerical gradients.

__4. Bridging the Gap: The Structural Estimation Paradigm__
text: ## __4. Bridging the Gap: The Structural Estimation Paradigm__ Modern empirical economics rarely chooses between pure ungrounded theory and pure unstructured data optimization. Instead, the standard paradigm is __Structural Estimation__ (e.g., using Mathematical Programming with Equilibrium Constraints, or MPEC). In this framework, the researcher assumes a flexible functional form (like a normalized quadratic or a random-coefficients logit) but treats the structural parameters as unknowns to be estimated. The algorithm nests the firm's or consumer's analytical optimization problem *inside* an empirical optimization loop (such as Maximum Likelihood or Generalized Method of Moments). The external loop optimizes over the parameter space to find the values that make the analytically derived optimal choices match the observed empirical distribution as closely as possible.
